# OMB M-25-22 — Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government

> **Federal policy, not NASA governance: binding on agencies as federal policy, a separate
> question from what NASA's own directives require.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary.
> It never by itself establishes what a specific NASA directive requires, and must not be
> cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | Office of Management and Budget (OMB), Executive Office of the President; signed by OMB Director Russell T. Vought |
| **Kind** | Policy memo (OMB Memorandum) |
| **Status** | Dated and effective April 3, 2025 [p.1]. Verified in the document text: "This memorandum rescinds and replaces OMB Memorandum M-24-18, Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government" [p.1, Overview]. Currently in force. |
| **Where to get it** | whitehouse.gov (OMB memoranda), free public. Public copy, confirmed anonymously off-network on 2026-10-26: `https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/M-25-22-Driving-Efficient-Acquisition-of-Artificial-Intelligence-in-Government.pdf` |
| **Binds whom** | Verbatim: "Covered Agencies. Except as specifically noted, this memorandum applies to all agencies defined in 44 U.S.C. § 3502(1)... The requirements in this memorandum do not apply to elements of the Intelligence Community" [p.2, Sec. 2, Scope] |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** (our reading) This is the procurement counterpart to M-25-21: M-25-21 sets what an agency must do once it uses high-impact AI, this memo governs how an agency should buy AI systems and services in the first place (vendor terms, authorization to operate, sunset planning). It is useful for seeing what the federal government requires of agency AI acquisitions generally; it says nothing about what any specific NASA directive requires.

**Key content for artificial intelligence / machine-learning assurance.**
- [p.7] Sec. 4(a): "Determining the Use of High-Impact AI. During this phase, agencies must identify reasonably foreseeable use cases arising from the use of an AI system or service, and to the greatest extent practicable, make an initial determination of whether a system is likely to host high-impact AI use cases, as defined by OMB Memorandum M-25-21."
- [p.9] Sec. 4(c): "OMB Memorandum M-25-21 Compliance Requirements. Contracts must ensure compliance with minimum risk management practices for high-impact use cases as required under M-25-21."
- [p.11] Sec. 4(e): "Authorization To Operate Compliance. Consistent with the requirements of OMB Circular No. A-130... any AI systems and services operated as an information system by or on behalf of an agency must receive an authorization to operate from an appropriate agency official prior to deployment."
- [p.6] Sec. 3: "The Chief AI Officer Council will periodically review agency processes to encourage best practices and interagency harmonization" — a monitoring role for the Council rather than a new agency-level CAIO duty (the CAIO role itself is created in M-25-21, not here).
- [p.2] Sec. 2: a permanent, non-waivable contractual prohibition requiring agencies to protect against vendors training their own commercial models on non-public agency data without consent.
- No independent definition of "high-impact AI" or Chief AI Officer appears in this memo; both are incorporated by reference to M-25-21, as the quotes above show.
- AI touchpoints found by keyword grep: pervasive, as expected for an AI-acquisition memo — "AI" and "artificial intelligence" throughout the acquisition-lifecycle sections; "automat..." in the context of automated monitoring/testing; "algorithm" and "machine learning" are not used as defined terms.

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** No direct counterpart on the current NASA document list; federal agency policy and NASA's own internal directives are kept as separate coverage axes in this project (our reading) — the nearest topical neighbor would be NPR 7120.5F (NASA's program/project management requirements, which govern acquisition-lifecycle decisions), but it answers a different question (what NASA requires of its own program/project acquisitions vs. what federal policy requires of agency AI procurement generally).
